title: Refugees find help in David-Horodok
summary: Accounts of arrivals and practical aid show how the community responded to people fleeing wartime violence.

editorialConnections.recordTitle: Refugee movement and aid in David-Horodok

editorialContent:
## A river town becomes a place of refuge

During the First World War, David-Horodok was far from the main fronts. But, as the memorial book recalls, distance did not spare the town from the consequences of war. In its account of the [Jewish refugees]( /communities/david-horodok/records/mention_d420a73ba653b840dc45b70f ) arriving in town, it describes people driven from their homes by Russian military orders and reaching David-Horodok hungry, cold, and without adequate clothing. A broader event record likewise captures arrivals and aid, though it cautions that several movements and groups may have been combined in the retelling. The book’s heading identifies the episode as belonging to the First World War, and its account sets the expulsions against the wartime years 1914–1917. ([jewishgen.org](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/david-gorodek/dav092.html))

One witness remembers an especially large arrival: a steamboat called the *Parachad* brought more than a hundred refugees at once. The translation says they came from Minsk. That detail differs from the supplied record summary, which says Pinsk; the memorial-book passage itself identifies Pinsk as the place where Yehuda Kashtan approached the regional committee, not as the refugees’ departure point. The account therefore supports the number and the arrival by steamboat more firmly than it settles the refugees’ origin. They were not, in any case, a single isolated group: the book also recalls refugees arriving in other movements. ([jewishgen.org](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/david-gorodek/dav092.html))

## From the synagogue to private homes

The town’s response began with shelter. The [Stolin Hasidic synagogue](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_acf0b86bb0c4e62f357cbf9f) opened its doors, while its congregation agreed to pray in the [Great Synagogue](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_6fd42f25769dd27a22f8d875) for the Sabbath. Within days, according to the witness, the refugees had also found places in residents’ homes. Food and dishes were collected, and the welcome extended beyond emergency lodging: the account emphasizes the warmth with which households received people who had been uprooted. The river that carried ordinary traffic between David-Horodok and the outside world had, in this moment, become a route by which displaced families arrived seeking help. ([jewishgen.org](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/david-gorodek/dav092.html))

The work was organized as well as spontaneous. [Yehuda Kashtan](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_6ec261d32d61235468170e54), a young local, had quietly gone to the [Regional Committee in Pinsk](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_1b684d53c76252cda111bcd4) and urged it to send refugees to his town, where they could be cared for. The witness presents him as the effort’s chief organizer: he arranged shelter, found ways to raise money, and persuaded others to act. [Jacob Rabinowitz](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_4ae06d67b6c1b35f58002960), a prominent householder, served on the new [Municipal Relief Committee](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_030adf323b278f0ffce80323); Rabbi [Boruchl](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_4633b1f4160e0635859e67a5) stood at its head. The memorial account thus remembers relief not as charity from a single benefactor, but as shared civic responsibility, drawing in householders, young people, religious leaders, and ordinary families. ([jewishgen.org](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/david-gorodek/dav092.html))

## Giving became communal work

Kashtan and Cantor Shmerl Lansky turned the synagogue into a place of organized fundraising. A special Sabbath service with a choir drew a large congregation; Torah honors and blessings for donors were offered, and the proceeds went to the refugees. Nearby Rubel joined the effort. Lansky and singers traveled there, where local congregations pledged money and donated food; a wagon carried the gifts back to David-Horodok. In summer, a speaker named Zaitchik addressed villagers to encourage further contributions. The account does not provide a total for the money or provisions raised, but it describes repeated efforts over the winter and summer rather than a one-time collection. ([jewishgen.org](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/david-gorodek/dav092.html))

The memorial book’s references to the [Joint](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_895931a6c0d7cf35009c4ecc) and to food-and-clothing distributions belong to a wider history of communal assistance and should not be treated as proof that the Joint organized this particular First World War operation. In the refugee episode itself, the witness names the local committee, the synagogue fundraising, and assistance from Rubel. The book separately recalls American committee relief after the First World War, including goods and clothing for the poor, and an orphanage established in a later phase of civic activity. These are related chapters in local mutual aid, but not the same event. ([jewishgen.org](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/Davyd-Haradok/dav001.html?utm_source=openai))

## What the wider record adds

This account belongs to the wider upheaval sometimes called *bieżeństwo*: the mass flight and forced evacuation of civilians from the western lands of the Russian Empire as German forces advanced in 1915. The scale was vast, and the journeys could mean hunger, exposure, and illness. That context helps explain why refugees arriving in David-Horodok needed more than a night’s lodging. But the memorial book tells us specifically what its witnesses remembered here: a steamboat arrival, shelter in a synagogue and homes, food collections, and sustained local organization. Wider accounts of wartime displacement cannot independently verify the town’s particular episode. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bie%C5%BCe%C5%84stwo))

A later crisis offers a revealing, though not identical, comparison. Yad Vashem’s study of Pinsk describes Jewish refugees arriving there after war broke out in 1939; residents took them into homes and provided food and shelter, while Soviet authorities restricted their ability to stay. It also draws on migration cards that record some two thousand Jews passing through Pinsk. That independent evidence concerns a different war and a different city, not confirmation of the David-Horodok testimony. It does, however, show that refuge and aid remained recurring realities in this border region—and that the routes and records of displaced people extended beyond what any one town’s memorial could preserve. ([wwv.yadvashem.org](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/odot_pdf/Microsoft%20Word%20-%202283.pdf))

The witness ends by seeing refugee relief as an early arena in which David-Horodok’s communal consciousness took practical form. The episode’s legacy lies in the actions it names: Kashtan’s initiative, the committee led by Rabbi Boruchl, Rabinowitz and the townspeople, the synagogue that made room, and the households that shared food and shelter. The testimony is not a complete register of the people who arrived or the paths they later took. It is a local memory of what the community chose to do when strangers, made vulnerable by war, reached its river town seeking safety. ([jewishgen.org](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/david-gorodek/dav092.html))
